On the mixed metric dimension of 22-connected graphs

Shi Chen and Xuanlong Ma Note: Corresponding author Affiliation: School of Science, Xi’an Petroleum University, Xi’an 710065, P. R. China
Abstract

We show that for a 22-connected graph GG which is not a cycle, the mixed metric dimension of GG is at most 2​c​(G)2c(G), where c⁡(G)c(G) is the cyclomatic number of GG. As an immediate application, we prove a conjecture proposed by Sedlar and Škrekovski (2021).

Keywords: Mixed metric dimension; Cyclomatic number; 22-connected graph

2020 MSC: 05C12; 05C38

†† E-mail addresses: nuoyoushi@gmail.com (Chen), xuanlma@xsyu.edu.cn (Ma)

1 Introduction

Every graph considered in our paper is finite, simple, and connected. Let GG be a graph. Denote by V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) the vertex set and edge set of GG, respectively. Let uu and vv be two vertices of GG. The distance between uu and vv is denoted by dG​(u,v){\rm d}_{G}(u,v), or simply by d⁡(u,v){\rm d}(u,v) when no confusion can arise. For distinct x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G), we say a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) distinguishes xx and yy whenever d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y).{\rm d}(v,x)\neq{\rm d}(v,y). A subset S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called a metric generator of GG if for every pair of distinct vertices x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G), there exists a vertex in SS such that this vertex distinguishes xx and yy. A metric generator of GG with minimum cardinality is called a metric basis of GG, and the cardinality of a metric basis is referred to as the metric dimension of GG. The concept of metric dimension was independently introduced in the 1970s by Harary and Melter [4] and Slater [13]. The aim is to distinguish vertices of a graph using distances. The metric dimension of a graph has a wide range of applications, including robot navigation in networks [8], chemistry [3], pattern recognition and image processing [10], and the game of Mastermind [1].

As a further variation of the classical notion of a metric generator, the concept of an edge metric generator was introduced in [7] to distinguish the edges of a graph by means of distances from a prescribed set of vertices. Although a metric basis of a connected graph GG uniquely determines every vertex of GG through its distance representation, it does not necessarily distinguish all edges of GG. This observation motivates the following definitions. For a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and an edge e={u,w}∈E⁡(G)e=\{u,w\}\in E(G), the distance between vv and ee is defined by d⁡(v,e)=min⁡{d⁡(v,u),d⁡(v,w)}.{\rm d}(v,e)=\min\{{\rm d}(v,u),{\rm d}(v,w)\}. A vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) is said to distinguish two distinct edges e1,e2∈E⁡(G)e_{1},e_{2}\in E(G) on condition that d⁡(x,e1)≠d⁡(x,e2).{\rm d}(x,e_{1})\neq{\rm d}(x,e_{2}). A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called an edge metric generator for GG provided that every pair of distinct edges of GG is distinguished by some vertex of SS. An edge metric generator of minimum cardinality is called an edge metric basis of GG, and its cardinality is called the edge metric dimension of GG.

Given a graph GG, we write

O⁡(G)=V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G).O(G)=V(G)\cup E(G).

A vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) is said to distinguish two distinct elements x,y∈O⁡(G)x,y\in O(G) (vertices or edges) if d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y).{\rm d}(v,x)\neq{\rm d}(v,y). A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called a mixed metric generator for GG if for every pair of distinct elements x,y∈O⁡(G)x,y\in O(G), there exists a vertex of SS such that it can distinguish x,yx,y. The cardinality of a mixed metric generator with minimum size, denoted by dimm​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G), is called the mixed metric dimension of GG. The mixed metric dimension of a graph was first introduced in [6]. For a comprehensive overview of the variants of metric dimension and their applications to network detection, graph isomorphism, coin-weighing problems, and machine learning, we refer the reader to the two surveys [9, 14].

In [6], the authors determined the mixed metric dimension of several families of graphs, including cycles, complete bipartite graphs, trees, and grid graphs. They also showed that the problem of determining the mixed metric dimension of a graph is NP-hard in the general case. A leaf of GG is a vertex with degree 11. Equivalently, a leaf of GG is a vertex of GG that is incident to exactly one edge. Denote by ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) the number of all leaves of GG. The cyclomatic number of GG, denoted by c⁡(G)c(G), is the number of independent cycles of GG. Namely

c⁡(G)=|E⁡(G)|−|V⁡(G)|+1.c(G)=|E(G)|-|V(G)|+1.

In [12], Sedlar and Škrekovski obtained the exact value of the mixed metric dimension of a unicyclic graph and they proposed the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.1

([12, Conjecture 13]) Let GG be a connected graph which is not a cycle. Then dimm​(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq\ell(G)+2c(G).

Conjecture 1.1 holds for trees and 33-connected graphs, see [12]. In [11], the authors showed that Conjecture 1.1 holds for all Theta graphs. Recently, Chakraborty, Foucaud, and Hakanen [2] proved that Conjecture 1.1 holds for a connected graph which is not a tree such that ℓ⁡(G)≥1\ell(G)\geq 1, and a connected graph GG with ℓ⁡(G)=0\ell(G)=0 and has a cut-vertex. In [5], the authors gave some graphs satisfying Conjecture 1.1. In this paper, we will prove the following theorem:

Theorem 1.2

Let GG be a 22-connected graph which is not a cycle. Then

dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G).{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G).

As an immediate application of Theorem 1.2, we confirm Conjecture 1.1.

2 Preliminaries

Let GG be a graph. A thread in a graph GG is a path whose internal vertices all have degree 22 in GG. Let P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}) be a thread of GG. We use G−P0G-P^{0} to denote the subgraph of GG that is obtained by removing the internal vertices of this thread PP and keeping the endpoints p0p_{0} and plp_{l}. For convenience, throughout this paper, we denote the vertex pip_{i} of PP by [i,i][i,i], and the edge {pj,pj+1}\{p_{j},p_{j+1}\} of PP by [j,j+1][j,j+1], where 0≤i≤l0\leq i\leq l and 0≤j≤l−10\leq j\leq l-1. Namely, every element of PP can be expressed as

[a,b],b−a∈{0,1},0≤a≤b≤l.[a,b],~~b-a\in\{0,1\},~~0\leq a\leq b\leq l.

If G−P0G-P^{0} is connected and l<dG−P0​(p0,pl)l<{\rm d}_{G-P^{0}}(p_{0},p_{l}), then PP is called a short thread of GG. If deg⁡(p0)≥3\deg(p_{0})\geq 3 and deg⁡(pl)≥3\deg(p_{l})\geq 3, then this thread PP is called maximal. By [15], a 22-connected graph which is not a cycle can be decomposed into distinct maximal threads. Write

ℬ={v∈V⁡(G):deg⁡(v)≥3}.\mathcal{B}=\{v\in V(G):\deg(v)\geq 3\}.
Lemma 2.1

Let GG be a graph with a u,vu,v-thread PP of length ll. If there exists z∉V⁡(P)z\notin V(P) such that d⁡(u,z)+d⁡(v,z)≤l{\rm d}(u,z)+{\rm d}(v,z)\leq l, then every shortest path from uu to zz does not pass through any internal vertex of PP.

Proof. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there exists a shortest path from uu to zz pass through some internal vertex of PP. Then clearly, d⁡(u,z)=l+d⁡(v,z){\rm d}(u,z)=l+{\rm d}(v,z). It follows that l+2​d​(v,z)=d⁡(u,z)+d⁡(v,z)≤ll+2{\rm d}(v,z)={\rm d}(u,z)+{\rm d}(v,z)\leq l, which is impossible as d⁡(v,z)≠0{\rm d}(v,z)\neq 0. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Lemma 2.2

Let GG be a graph with a u,vu,v-thread PP of length ll. If there exists an edge e={a,b}∈E⁡(G)∖E⁡(P)e=\{a,b\}\in E(G)\setminus E(P) such that d⁡(u,e)+d⁡(v,e)≤l−1{\rm d}(u,e)+{\rm d}(v,e)\leq l-1, then there exists a u,vu,v-path WW in G−P0G-P^{0} such that |W|≤l|W|\leq l.

Proof. Assume that d⁡(u,e)=d⁡(u,u′){\rm d}(u,e)={\rm d}(u,u^{\prime}) and d⁡(v,e)=d⁡(v,v′){\rm d}(v,e)={\rm d}(v,v^{\prime}), where u′,v′∈{a,b}u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\in\{a,b\}.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that there exists a shortest path from uu to u′u^{\prime} pass through some internal vertex of PP. Then we have that d⁡(u,u′)=l+d⁡(v,u′){\rm d}(u,u^{\prime})=l+{\rm d}(v,u^{\prime}). Note that d⁡(v,u′)≥d⁡(v,e){\rm d}(v,u^{\prime})\geq{\rm d}(v,e). It follows that

d⁡(u,e)+d⁡(v,e)=d⁡(u,u′)+d⁡(v,v′)=l+d⁡(v,u′)+d⁡(v,v′)≤l−1,{\rm d}(u,e)+{\rm d}(v,e)={\rm d}(u,u^{\prime})+{\rm d}(v,v^{\prime})=l+{\rm d}(v,u^{\prime})+{\rm d}(v,v^{\prime})\leq l-1,

which is a contradiction. We conclude that every shortest path from uu to u′u^{\prime} do not pass through any internal vertex of PP. Similarly, every shortest path from vv to v′v^{\prime} do not pass through any internal vertex of PP.

Take now a shortest path from uu to u′u^{\prime} and a shortest path from vv to u′u^{\prime}. If u′=v′u^{\prime}=v^{\prime}, then we concatenate the two paths at u′u^{\prime} to obtain a u,vu,v-path, say WW, which implies that WW in G−P0G-P^{0} and |W|=d⁡(u,e)+d⁡(v,e)≤l−1<l|W|={\rm d}(u,e)+{\rm d}(v,e)\leq l-1<l, as desired. If u′≠v′u^{\prime}\neq v^{\prime}, then we obtain the u,vu,v-path of G−P0G-P^{0} has length d⁡(u,e)+d⁡(v,e)+1≤l{\rm d}(u,e)+{\rm d}(v,e)+1\leq l, as wanted. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Lemma 2.3

Let GG be a 22-connected graph without leaves. Then |ℬ|≤2​c​(G)−2|\mathcal{B}|\leq 2c(G)-2.

Proof. It is well known that ∑v∈V⁡(G)deg⁡(v)=2​|E⁡(G)|\sum_{v\in V(G)}\deg(v)=2|E(G)|. Note that GG has no leaves. We deduce that

∑v∈V⁡(G)(deg⁡(v)−2)=∑v∈V⁡(G)deg⁡(v)−2​|V⁡(G)|=2​(|E⁡(G)|−|V⁡(G)|)=2​c​(G)−2.\sum_{v\in V(G)}(\deg(v)-2)=\sum_{v\in V(G)}\deg(v)-2|V(G)|=2(|E(G)|-|V(G)|)=2c(G)-2.

It follows that |ℬ|≤∑v∈V⁡(G)(deg⁡(v)−2)=2​c​(G)−2,|\mathcal{B}|\leq\sum_{v\in V(G)}(\deg(v)-2)=2c(G)-2, as desired. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Lemma 2.4

Let GG be a graph with a thread P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}), where p0=up_{0}=u and pl=vp_{l}=v. Suppose that H=G−P0H=G-P^{0} is connected and l≥dH​(u,v)l\geq{\rm d}_{H}(u,v). Then

dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2.{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2.

In particular, if ℛ\mathcal{R} is a mixed metric generator of HH, then ℛ∪{u,w}\mathcal{R}\cup\{u,w\} is a mixed metric generator of GG, where w=p⌈l/2⌉w=p_{\lceil l/2\rceil}.

Proof. Write d=dH​(u,v)d={\rm d}_{H}(u,v). We first claim that for any pair of vertices a,b∈V⁡(H)a,b\in V(H), dH​(a,b)=dG​(a,b){\rm d}_{H}(a,b)={\rm d}_{G}(a,b). Indeed, dG​(a,b)≤dH​(a,b){\rm d}_{G}(a,b)\leq{\rm d}_{H}(a,b). In GG, if there exists a shortest path from aa to bb that avoids the internal vertices of PP, then dG​(a,b)=dH​(a,b){\rm d}_{G}(a,b)={\rm d}_{H}(a,b), as desired. Otherwise, every shortest path from aa to bb must contain an internal vertex of PP. Since PP is a thread, it follows that every shortest path from aa to bb must pass through all internal vertices of PP, which implies any shortest path from aa to bb contains the entire PP. Now, notice that HH is connected and l≥dl\geq d. It follows that dG​(a,b)≥dH​(a,b){\rm d}_{G}(a,b)\geq{\rm d}_{H}(a,b), and so we have dG​(a,b)=dH​(a,b){\rm d}_{G}(a,b)={\rm d}_{H}(a,b). We conclude that the above claim is valid.

Now, let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a mixed metric generator of HH with the smallest cardinality, that is |ℛ|=dimm​(H)|\mathcal{R}|={\rm dim_{m}}(H). Without loss of generality, we may assume that there exists r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} such that dH​(r,u)≥dH​(r,v){\rm d}_{H}(r,u)\geq{\rm d}_{H}(r,v). Write

A=dH​(r,u),B=dH​(r,v),δr=A−B,A={\rm d}_{H}(r,u),~~B={\rm d}_{H}(r,v),~~\delta_{r}=A-B,

then δr≥0\delta_{r}\geq 0. Furthermore, any element of PP can be represented as

z=[a,b],b−a∈{0,1},0≤a≤b≤l.z=[a,b],~~b-a\in\{0,1\},~~0\leq a\leq b\leq l.

Note that d=dH​(u,v)d={\rm d}_{H}(u,v). It follows that

dG​(u,z)=min⁡{a,d+l−b}{\rm d}_{G}(u,z)=\min\{a,d+l-b\} (1)

and

dG​(r,z)=min⁡{A+a,B+l−b}=B+min⁡{δr+a,l−b}.{\rm d}_{G}(r,z)=\min\{A+a,B+l-b\}=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+a,l-b\}. (2)

Now let m=⌈l2⌉m=\lceil\frac{l}{2}\rceil and let w=pmw=p_{m}. Then

dG(w,z)={m−b,if b≤m;a−m,if a≥m.{\rm d}_{G}(w,z)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}m-b,&\hbox{if $b\leq m$;}\\ a-m,&\hbox{if $a\geq m$.}\end{array}\right. (3)

Claim 1. Any two distinct elements of PP are distinguished by some vertex of {w,u,r}\{w,u,r\}.

We say that an element [a,b][a,b] of PP lies on the left (resp. right) side of ww if b≤mb\leq m (resp. a≥ma\geq m). Naturally, the element [m,m][m,m] of PP lies on both the left and the right sides of ww. In the following, we consider two cases.

Case 1. The two distinct elements of PP lie on the same side of ww.

If the two distinct elements of PP lie on the left side of ww, then by (1) and (3), we see that the two distinct elements are distinguished by some vertex of {u,w}\{u,w\}, as desired. Suppose now that the two distinct elements of PP lie on the right side of ww, say [a,b][a,b] and [x,y][x,y]. If a≠xa\neq x, then ww can distinguish them by (3). In the following, assume a=xa=x. Then by (2), we have that

dG​(r,[a,b])=B+min⁡{δr+a,l−b},dG​(r,[x,y])=B+min⁡{δr+a,l−y}.{\rm d}_{G}(r,[a,b])=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+a,l-b\},~~{\rm d}_{G}(r,[x,y])=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+a,l-y\}. (4)

Since y≥ay\geq a, b≥ab\geq a, and 2​a≥l2a\geq l, we have that a≥l−a≥l−ba\geq l-a\geq l-b and a≥l−ya\geq l-y. Note that b≠yb\neq y. It follows from (4) that [a,b][a,b] and [x,y][x,y] are distinguished by rr, as desired.

Case 2. The two distinct elements [a,b][a,b] and [x,y][x,y] of PP lie on opposite sides side of ww.

Without loss of generality, assume that z1=[a,b]z_{1}=[a,b] lies on the left side of ww and z2=[x,y]z_{2}=[x,y] lies on the right side of ww. Namely, b≤m≤xb\leq m\leq x. From (1), it follows that dG​(u,z1)=min⁡{a,d+l−b}=a{\rm d}_{G}(u,z_{1})=\min\{a,d+l-b\}=a and dG​(u,z2)=min⁡{x,d+l−y}{\rm d}_{G}(u,z_{2})=\min\{x,d+l-y\}. If a≠min⁡{x,d+l−y}a\neq\min\{x,d+l-y\}, then z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are distinguished by uu, as desired. Thus, in the following, we assume that

a=min⁡{x,d+l−y}.a=\min\{x,d+l-y\}. (5)

Suppose that a=xa=x. Then z1=[m,m]=wz_{1}=[m,m]=w and z2=[m,m+1]z_{2}=[m,m+1]. We deduce that z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} lie on the right side of ww, and so Case 1 ends the proof.

We next suppose that a<xa<x. If b=yb=y, then y=b≤m≤x≤yy=b\leq m\leq x\leq y, which implies that z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} lie on the left side of ww, and so Case 1 completes our proof. Thus, in the following, assume that b≠yb\neq y, that is, y>by>b. Now, in view of (2), we have that

dG​(r,z1)=B+min⁡{δr+a,l−b},dG​(r,z2)=B+min⁡{δr+x,l−y}.{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{1})=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+a,l-b\},~~{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{2})=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+x,l-y\}.

It follows from (5) that a=d+l−ya=d+l-y. Since d≥1d\geq 1 and δr≥0\delta_{r}\geq 0, we conclude that

l−y=a−d<a<x≤x+δr.l-y=a-d<a<x\leq x+\delta_{r}.

As a result, we have dG​(r,z2)=B+l−y{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{2})=B+l-y. If dG​(r,z1)=B+l−b{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{1})=B+l-b, then clearly, dG​(r,z1)≠dG​(r,z2){\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{1})\neq{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{2}), and so z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are distinguished by rr, as wanted. Otherwise, dG​(r,z1)=B+δr+a{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{1})=B+\delta_{r}+a. Consequently, we have

B+δr+a−(B+l−y)=δr+a−(a−d)=δr+d>0.B+\delta_{r}+a-(B+l-y)=\delta_{r}+a-(a-d)=\delta_{r}+d>0.

This forces that dG​(r,z1)≠dG​(r,z2){\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{1})\neq{\rm d}_{G}(r,z_{2}), which implies that z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are distinguished by rr, as required. Thus, Claim 11 is valid.

Claim 2. For any two elements z∈O⁡(P)∖O⁡(H)z\in O(P)\setminus O(H) and z′∈O⁡(H)z^{\prime}\in O(H), there exists an element in {u,w}∪ℛ\{u,w\}\cup\mathcal{R} such that it can distinguish zz and z′z^{\prime}.

Note that PP is a thread. It follows that

dG​(w,z′)=min⁡{m+dH​(u,z′),l−m+dH​(v,z′)}≥l−m.{\rm d}_{G}(w,z^{\prime})=\min\{m+{\rm d}_{H}(u,z^{\prime}),l-m+{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})\}\geq l-m. (6)

If l=2​kl=2k for some positive integer kk, then dG​(w,z)≤k−1{\rm d}_{G}(w,z)\leq k-1 and dG​(w,z′)≥k{\rm d}_{G}(w,z^{\prime})\geq k, which implies that ww distinguishes zz and z′z^{\prime}, as required.

In the following, we assume that l=2​k+1≥3l=2k+1\geq 3 for some positive integer kk, that is, m=k+1m=k+1. Then by (3) and (6), it is easy to see that if z∉{[1,1],[0,1]}z\notin\{[1,1],[0,1]\}, then zz and z′z^{\prime} are distinguished by ww. In the following, we consider two cases.

Case 1. z=[1,1]z=[1,1].

Indeed, we may assume that ww does not distinguish zz and z′z^{\prime}. It follows that

dG​(w,z′)=dG​(w,z)=k.{\rm d}_{G}(w,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{G}(w,z)=k.

In view of (6), it can be inferred that l−m+dH​(v,z′)=k+dH​(v,z′)=kl-m+{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})=k+{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})=k, and hence dH​(v,z′)=0{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})=0. Now, by (2), we have that

dG​(r,z)=B+min⁡{δr+1,l−1}≥B+1.{\rm d}_{G}(r,z)=B+\min\{\delta_{r}+1,l-1\}\geq B+1.

However, because of dH​(v,z′)=0{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})=0, we have dG​(r,z′)≤B{\rm d}_{G}(r,z^{\prime})\leq B. It follows that rr distinguishes zz and z′z^{\prime}, as desired.

Case 2. z=[0,1]z=[0,1].

Clearly, we may assume that both ww and uu do not distinguish zz and z′z^{\prime}. Therefore, we have dG​(u,z′)=dG​(u,z)=0{\rm d}_{G}(u,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{G}(u,z)=0, which means dG​(u,z′)=dH​(u,z′)=0{\rm d}_{G}(u,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{H}(u,z^{\prime})=0. Moreover, we also have dG​(w,z′)=dG​(w,z)=k{\rm d}_{G}(w,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{G}(w,z)=k by (3). Now

dG​(w,z′)=min⁡{k+1+dH​(u,z′),k+dH​(v,z′)}=k=k+dH​(v,z′){\rm d}_{G}(w,z^{\prime})=\min\{k+1+{\rm d}_{H}(u,z^{\prime}),k+{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})\}=k=k+{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})

implies dH​(v,z′)=0{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})=0. As a consequence, dH​(v,z′)=dH​(u,z′)=0{\rm d}_{H}(v,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{H}(u,z^{\prime})=0. We conclude that z′={u,v}∈E⁡(G)z^{\prime}=\{u,v\}\in E(G), that is, dG​(u,v)=dH​(u,v)=1{\rm d}_{G}(u,v)={\rm d}_{H}(u,v)=1. It follows that there exists a vertex q∈ℛq\in\mathcal{R} such that qq can distinguish uu and z′z^{\prime}. Consequently, dH​(q,u)≠dH​(q,z′){\rm d}_{H}(q,u)\neq{\rm d}_{H}(q,z^{\prime}), which forces dH​(q,z′)=dH​(q,v){\rm d}_{H}(q,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{H}(q,v). Hence, we must have dH​(q,v)<dH​(q,u){\rm d}_{H}(q,v)<{\rm d}_{H}(q,u). Now

dG​(q,z)=min⁡{dH​(q,u),dH​(q,v)+l−1}>dH​(q,v)=dH​(q,z′)=dG​(q,z′){\rm d}_{G}(q,z)=\min\{{\rm d}_{H}(q,u),{\rm d}_{H}(q,v)+l-1\}>{\rm d}_{H}(q,v)={\rm d}_{H}(q,z^{\prime})={\rm d}_{G}(q,z^{\prime})

implies that qq distinguishes zz and z′z^{\prime}, as desired. Thus, Claim 22 holds.

Now note that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a mixed metric generator of HH with the smallest cardinality. Combining Claims 11 and 22, we have that ℛ∪{u,w}\mathcal{R}\cup\{u,w\} is a mixed metric generator of GG. It follows that dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Lemma 2.5

Let GG be a 22-connected graph which is not a cycle. If every thread of GG is short, then ℬ\mathcal{B} is a mixed metric generator of GG.

Proof. Take distinct z,w∈O⁡(G)z,w\in O(G). It suffices to show that there exists an element of ℬ\mathcal{B} such that it can distinguish zz and ww. We consider three cases as follows.

Case 1. zz and ww lie on the same thread, and z,w∉ℬz,w\notin\mathcal{B}.

Take a maximal thread P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}) of GG, let p0=up_{0}=u and pl=vp_{l}=v. Then u,v∈ℬu,v\in\mathcal{B} and l<dH​(u,v)l<{\rm d}_{H}(u,v), where H=G−P0H=G-P^{0} is connected. Now assume that z,w∈O⁡(P)∖{u,v}z,w\in O(P)\setminus\{u,v\}. Note that

dG​(u,[i,i])=i,dG​(v,[i,i])=l−i,0≤i≤l,{\rm d}_{G}(u,[i,i])=i,~~{\rm d}_{G}(v,[i,i])=l-i,~~0\leq i\leq l,

and

dG​(u,[j−1,j])=j−1,dG​(v,[j−1,j])=l−j,1≤j≤l.{\rm d}_{G}(u,[j-1,j])=j-1,~~{\rm d}_{G}(v,[j-1,j])=l-j,~~1\leq j\leq l.

It follows that z,wz,w must be distinguished by some element of {u,v}\{u,v\}, as desired.

Case 2. One zz and ww belongs to ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Without loss of generality, let w∈ℬw\in\mathcal{B}. If zz is a vertex or an edge which is not incident with ww, then dG​(w,z)>0{\rm d}_{G}(w,z)>0, which implies that zz and ww are distinguished by ww, as required. Thus, in the following, we may assume that zz is an edge incident with ww. Note that deg⁡(w)≥3\deg(w)\geq 3. Starting from ww, we can obtain a maximal thread QQ containing zz. Let w′w^{\prime} be the other endpoint of this maximal thread and let the length of QQ be ss. Then w′∈ℬw^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B} and s≤dG−Q0​(w,w′)s\leq{\rm d}_{G-Q^{0}}(w,w^{\prime}). We conclude that

dG​(w′,w)=s,dG​(w′,z)=s−1.{\rm d}_{G}(w^{\prime},w)=s,~~{\rm d}_{G}(w^{\prime},z)=s-1.

As a result, zz and ww are distinguished by w′w^{\prime}, as required.

Case 3. zz and ww lie on distinct threads, and z,w∉ℬz,w\notin\mathcal{B}.

Let zz lies on the maximal thread P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}) of GG, and let p0=u,pl=vp_{0}=u,p_{l}=v. In the following, we may assume that both uu and vv do not distinguish zz and ww. Namely,

dG​(u,z)=dG​(u,w),dG​(v,z)=dG​(v,w).{\rm d}_{G}(u,z)={\rm d}_{G}(u,w),~~{\rm d}_{G}(v,z)={\rm d}_{G}(v,w). (7)

As a result, we have that

dG(u,z)+dG(v,z)={l,if z is a vertex;l−1,if z is an edge.{\rm d}_{G}(u,z)+{\rm d}_{G}(v,z)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}l,&\hbox{if $z$ is a vertex;}\\ l-1,&\hbox{if $z$ is an edge.}\end{array}\right. (8)

Suppose, for contradiction, that ww is a vertex. Then by (7) and (8), we deduce that dG​(u,w)+dG​(v,w)=l{\rm d}_{G}(u,w)+{\rm d}_{G}(v,w)=l. Note that w∉O⁡(P)w\notin O(P). Now Lemma 2.1 implies that dG−P0​(u,v)≤l{\rm d}_{G-P^{0}}(u,v)\leq l, this contradicts that PP is short.

We conclude that ww is an edge. Similarly, we can also obtain that zz is an edge. Applying (7) and (8) again, we know that dG​(u,w)+dG​(v,w)=l−1{\rm d}_{G}(u,w)+{\rm d}_{G}(v,w)=l-1. It follows from Lemma 2.2 that there exists a path in G−P0G-P^{0} such that its length is at most ll. This forces dG−P0​(u,v)≤l{\rm d}_{G-P^{0}}(u,v)\leq l, which contradicts that PP is short. Thus, one of uu and vv must distinguish zz and ww, as wanted.

Now, combining the above three cases, we conclude that the required result is valid. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

3 Proof of the Main Result

In this section, we will show Theorem 1.2 and confirm Conjecture 1.1. We begin by citing three known results.

Theorem 3.1

([2, Corollary 16]) Let GG be a connected graph which is not a tree such that ℓ⁡(G)≥1\ell(G)\geq 1. Then dimm​(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq\ell(G)+2c(G).

Theorem 3.2

([6, Theorem 4.3]) Let GG be a tree. Then dimm​(G)=ℓ​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)=\ell(G).

Theorem 3.3

([2, Corollary 12(i)]) Let GG be a connected graph with ℓ⁡(G)=0\ell(G)=0. If GG has a cut-vertex, then dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G).

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2. Note that GG is not a cycle and ℓ⁡(G)=0\ell(G)=0. Then c⁡(G)≥2c(G)\geq 2. If every thread of GG is short, then by Lemmas 2.3 and 2.5, we have that

dimm​(G)≤|ℬ|≤2​c​(G)−2≤2​c​(G),{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq|\mathcal{B}|\leq 2c(G)-2\leq 2c(G),

as desired.

In the following, we may assume that GG has a maximal thread P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}) such that dG−P0​(u,v)≤l{\rm d}_{G-P^{0}}(u,v)\leq l. Now let H=G−P0H=G-P^{0}. Clearly, HH is connected and has no leaves. It follows that

c⁡(H)=|E⁡(H)|−|V⁡(H)|+1=(|E⁡(G)|−l)−(|V⁡(G)|−(l−1))+1,c(H)=|E(H)|-|V(H)|+1=(|E(G)|-l)-(|V(G)|-(l-1))+1,

that is,

c⁡(G)=c⁡(H)+1.c(G)=c(H)+1. (9)

Suppose that HH is a cycle. Then c⁡(G)=2c(G)=2. Namely, GG is a graph in which p0p_{0} and plp_{l} are the only vertices of degree 33, while every other vertex has degree 22. It follows from [11, Corollaries 8 and 11] that dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G), as required.

In the following, suppose that HH is not a cycle. Assume that HH has a cut-vertex. Theorem 3.3 implies that dimm​(H)≤2​c​(H){\rm dim_{m}}(H)\leq 2c(H). Moreover, by Lemma 2.4 and (9), we deduce that dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2≤2​c​(H)+2=2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2\leq 2c(H)+2=2c(G), as wanted. Thus, next, we may assume that HH has no cut vertices. It follows that HH is 22-connected.

Note that HH is a 22-connected graph which is not a cycle. To complete the proof of this theorem, we now proceed by induction on c⁡(G)c(G). If c⁡(G)=2c(G)=2, then by (9), HH is a cycle, and so the result follows from the above proof.

Now suppose that c⁡(G)≥3c(G)\geq 3, and assume that the assertion holds for every graph G′G^{\prime} satisfying the hypotheses of the theorem with c⁡(G′)<c⁡(G)c(G^{\prime})<c(G). Note that HH satisfies the hypotheses of our theorem. In view of (9), by the induction hypothesis, we have dimm​(H)≤2​c​(H){\rm dim_{m}}(H)\leq 2c(H). Moreover, by Lemma 2.4, we conclude that

dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2≤2​c​(H)+2=2​c​(G).{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2\leq 2c(H)+2=2c(G).

This completes the induction and the proof. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Note that a 22-connected graph has no leaves. Now, combining Theorems 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, and 1.2, we conclude that Conjecture 1.1 holds for any connected graph which is not a cycle. Namely, Conjecture 1.1 is valid.
